subject: chopperMotorbike
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: custom chopper motorbike.
Style: Overwatch.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the chopper motorbike build in an Overwatch-inspired style using the SDK, thinking through the bold geometric shapes, hero color palette, and glowing accents. I need a proper joint hierarchy with a single root joint, like a "frame" joint, since the builder requires exactly one.

For dimensions and aesthetics, I'm settling on a Junkertown-style orange and black chopper with bright teal glow elements for the engine core, headlight, and underglow, plus hex-patterned decals and a stylized emblem, along with custom textures for things like the tire tread and speedometer gauge.

Now I'm mapping out wheel geometry using lathe revolves around the X-axis for the tire and rim profiles, with the front wheel narrower and the rear wheel fatter, and I'm figuring out how to construct spokes as a radial arrangement of thin rods around the wheel joint.

Still working out joint orientation...

For the frame, I'm planning the chopper's skeleton: a root "frame" joint, a "steer" joint at the fork neck, "wheelF" parented to steer, "wheelR" parented to frame, plus maybe a kickstand and throttle grip hinge.

Now I'm laying out the actual geometry in side view — placing the front wheel center around (0, 0.36, 1.15) with a 0.36 radius, and positioning the steering head near the top for that long raked chopper fork.

I settle on roughly a 36° rake angle, running the fork from about (0, 1.05, 0.62) at the triple tree down to the axle near (0, 0.36, 1.12), giving a fork length of about 0.85. Then I place the rear wheel at (0, 0.40, -0.85) with a fatter 0.40 radius and 0.26 width, and start sketching the hardtail frame running from the steering head back toward the seat and rear axle, with the V-twin engine with glowing cylinders sitting in the middle.

Now I'm working out the gas tank as a teardrop loft tapering from front to back, planning to paint it with cel orange and flame decals, then adding a low solo seat with black stitched leather and a sissy bar behind it. For the rear fender, I'm sweeping a thin elliptical profile along a curved path arcing over the rear wheel.

Front fender needs a similar treatment but wrapping tighter around the front wheel—I'm computing points along an arc from behind the wheel up to the front using angle-based position math, then feeding those into a catmull path, before moving on to the ape hanger handlebars.

Working out handlebar geometry...

Now I need to position the headlight bucket near the fork triple tree, mounted between the fork legs around y=0.92-0.98, with small mirror and brake levers near the grips.

Setting fork legs at x=±0.11 with wheel width 0.12 for proper clearance, with chrome upper tubes and darker lower sliders of different radii, plus triple tree boxes crossing at top and bottom to connect the fork legs.

I'm positioning the steering joint along the fork axis, then building out the frame geometry -- placing the head tube parallel to the fork direction, connecting it from the steer point down toward the axle with a chunky radius to match the Overwatch-style aesthetic.

Now I'm laying out the rest of the frame: top tube running from the head tube back to the seat post, down tube dropping to the engine cradle, and hardtail rear stays connecting the seat area and bottom frame to the rear axle on both sides.

I realize nearest-joint bone assignment could accidentally attach frame tubes to the steering bone instead of the frame, since the head tube sits close to the steering joint. To avoid this, I'll explicitly specify `bone: frame` on every frame-related part rather than relying on automatic nearest-bone logic.

Now I'm working out the V-twin engine layout: crankcase positioned near the frame center, with front and rear cylinders tilted outward at roughly symmetric angles from the crank to mimic a real V-twin silhouette, each built as a rod with cooling fin rings and painted a metal steel/iron color.

I'm adding cylinder heads with orange rocker covers, pushrod tubes, and a large chrome round air cleaner on the right side with a hex emblem for an Overwatch-style detail. For exhaust, I'm planning paired drag pipes sweeping from each cylinder's exhaust port down and back along the right side with a tapered end, using curved paths to get that classic side-pipe look.

Adding heat shield clamp rings along the pipes, then placing a glowing hexagonal teal energy core between the cylinders for that Overwatch-style accent.

Also adding glowing under-frame strips and neon rings inside the wheel rims for a hover-ish effect, then settling on a deep blue, orange, and cream color scheme inspired by Overwatch's palette.

I'm finalizing the color plan: bright orange tank and fenders with white hex stripes, dark gunmetal frame, cyan glow accents, brown leather seat with orange stitching, and chrome pipes. Now I'm sketching a staged base platform—leaning toward a rounded rectangular plate with a hex-tile pattern and glow ring rather than a round one, sized to fit the bike's length.

For positioning, I want to keep the base thin (~0.05-0.06) and let the wheels sink slightly into its top surface rather than fussing with offsetting every coordinate—simpler than wrapping all points through a height-shift function, even though it means the tires visually overlap the platform a bit.

With PL=0.04 the handlebar top lands around 1.52m, close to real chopper ape-hanger proportions. Now I'm planning scale and part count — aiming for 180-340 parts, several textures, and a substantial 600-800 line module, so I need to build efficiently while keeping detail rich.

I'm mapping out the builder API I'll rely on — joints, parts, sweeps, rods, lathes, extrudes, lofts, decals — and planning a tight ~25-color palette using cel() paints for things like chrome, cream, and navy so I stay under the flat-color limit.

For texture resolution, I'm estimating the texel density on an 8m² painted surface against the shared 1024 sheet, which works out to roughly 3mm per texel — plenty fine for the hand-painted, two-tone cel look I'm going for on this Overwatch-style vehicle. I'm deciding to use cel paints for the main lofts, sweeps, and lathes, flat color strings for tiny parts, and keeping glow-enabled parts as non-paint. Now I'm sketching out the tank body as a loft with stations placed along the z-axis, each defining a width and height.

I'm laying out five tank cross-section stations from front to back, adjusting their y-position, width, and height at each point to shape the teardrop profile sitting above the frame's top tube — wider in the middle, tapering at both ends. I'm also considering how the loft's cross-section defaults work, whether it needs explicit sides or section options, and then planning to add flame decals onto the tank's loft surface by specifying a point, direction, and size for each decal.

For the decal placement, I'm computing a surface hit point on the tank using an azimuth of 90 degrees to land on the side facing +X, then orienting the decal direction along that axis. I'm worried that mirroring for the opposite side (-X) could flip the flame artwork awkwardly, so I'm leaning toward a symmetric-looking flame design that reads fine on either side rather than trying to force exact mirroring, and avoiding any text in the decal to dodge that mirroring problem entirely.

So no mirror for the left side, mirror true for the right side, matching how the eye example used mirror relative to viewing direction. I'll trust this holds even after rotation is applied to the actual projection.

Rather than risk complications with a surface built from the loft, I'll use SVG decals placed on the tank geometry instead of trying to paint patterns directly. I'm sketching out a list of 5-12 textures to apply — starting with a flame decal for the tank side and a hexagonal emblem logo for the tank top or fender.

For the emblem, I'm designing a custom dark hexagon with orange border and a lightning bolt through the center, avoiding anything too close to existing branding. The remaining textures include a glowing concentric-ring headlight lens, a rasterized speedometer gauge texture for the handlebar mount, and tire tread detailing — the tread I'll generate through the paint function using angle and height parameters to create chevron-style blocks rather than a separate texture map.

Still working out the details: a diamond-quilted stitch pattern for the seat using a paint function based on diagonal coordinate sums, a rear license plate texture reading "OVERRUN", and hazard stripe decals painted diagonally in orange and black along the rear fender.

Now I'm planning the remaining decorative elements: a red hex taillight glow lens, a round air cleaner emblem with concentric fan-blade styling, and hex-tiled texture for the base platform, considering whether to use an SVG pattern or a plane geometry for that last piece.

I'm also cataloguing all the glowing parts across the model -- headlight, taillight, engine core, rim neon rings, exhaust tips, underglow strips, base ring, and amber turn signals -- while adding character flair like exaggerated chunky proportions, a fat rear tire, oversized tank and exhaust, and maybe a hanging chain or pennant flag off a sissy bar for that Overwatch-biker aesthetic.

Now I'm working out the pennant itself: using extruded paint stripes for a swallowtail flag since textures don't apply well to extrudes, and considering whether cards would work better since they're double-sided. I'm also adding small details like round ape-hanger mirrors, orange rubber grips, and front/rear brake discs made from thin lathed shapes with holes cut in.

For the drivetrain, I'm setting up front and rear sprockets using gear geometry — a 12-tooth front sprocket near the engine output and a 36-tooth rear sprocket on the wheel — then connecting them with two tangent rods to approximate a chain, and planning a bone on the rear wheel joint for spin animation.

Now I'm working out the x-axis positions so the sprocket, chain, and rear stays don't collide — placing the sprocket slightly outboard of the wheel hub, the chain just inside the stays, and positioning the stays themselves near the axle so everything clears the hub region. I'm defining the rear axle endpoints with nuts, then moving on to lay out the rear wheel center for the rest of the frame details.

Setting up helper functions and a color palette for the bike — defining a padding constant and a vector helper, then building out a set of cel-shaded colors (orange, navy, chrome-ish steel, black, cream, leather) to use across the parts.

Now I'm designing the custom tire paint logic: a dark rubber base with lighter tread lugs arranged in an alternating zigzag pattern around the tire's circumference, based on height and angle along the lathe surface.

For sidewall detail, I'm adding a thin orange/cream ring at a specific radial distance when the surface normal faces outward (|n.x|>0.6), computed using the radial distance from the axis.

Now I'm building a wheel-creation function that assembles the joint, lathed tire profile, rim, hub, spokes, disc brake, and neon ring, defining the tire's cross-section outline as a sequence of radius/width coordinate pairs to shape the sidewall curve and tread.

Checking that edge segments stay short enough that smoothing won't cause corners to cross, then confirming the lathe setup uses the x-axis with the outline distance as radius and height as the axis coordinate, with enough segments for roundness.

Now I'm designing the rim geometry as a lathed barrel profile with a slightly raised outer edge and visible inner lip, then considering whether to model the wheel as a spoked mag wheel with around nine rods plus a hub lathe for the center.

I'm trying out a simpler flat disc wheel with cut-out blades instead, going for a chunky turbine-style look rather than individual rods, using a small count of ring items as the blade placeholders.

Settling on 5 thick spokes radiating from a central hub cylinder, with the hub capped by a small orange disc, plus a lathe-turned brake disc profile on the inner face to suggest drilled ventilation.

Now I'm adding caliper boxes and planning a glowing neon ring built from a closed Catmull sweep around the rim, applied to both wheel faces and attached to the wheel joint bone. Each wheel ends up with roughly 18 parts total, and I'm moving on to fork details -- chrome stanchion rods from the tree down partway, then thicker slider rods down to the axle.

I'm working out the fork geometry: defining the tree position and front wheel axle point, then setting up a lerp helper to interpolate leg positions, adding ribbed rubber gaiter rings, fork brace, and fender mounts.

Setting up steer joint and handlebar rig...

Now I'm planning the full joint hierarchy: frame as root, then steer, wheelF, wheelR parented at frame, kickstand as a hinge off the frame, and considering extra joints like a grip twist or gearshift before settling on just adding a kickstand.

I'm figuring out the kickstand's rest pose — folded up rather than deployed, so the bike stays upright. I'm placing its pivot and foot coordinates while checking for collisions with the exhaust pipes positioned nearby on the frame.

Now I'm moving on to the engine details, planning the crankcase shape using a tapered box geometry stretched along the bike's width.

For the engine covers, I'm thinking a round primary cover on one side with a hex-glow emblem core, and a matching cover on the other side suggesting a belt housing.

Still designing hex texture and cylinder placement...

Positioning the rocker cover box at the head's center offset along the cylinder direction, aligning its orientation with the engine axis...

Now I'm figuring out placement for the chrome air cleaner on the right side, nudging its x-position so it clears the cylinder fins without overlapping.

I'm giving it a lathed dome shape with a textured circular emblem facing outward, then considering an optional oil tank or battery box under the seat and planning out the exhaust pipe geometry next.

Now I'm defining the frame tubes: computing the headtube rod position from interpolated points along the fork line, then plotting the top tube as a Catmull-Rom curve running from the headtube down through the tank area toward the rear seat region.

I'm moving on to the down tube and lower cradle rails, positioning them with interpolated points between the fork area and the engine, and setting up side rails offset from center to pass around the crankcase toward the rear axle.

Next I'm sketching the seat stays connecting the seat post down to the rear axle plates, and sketching a hardtail rear section with dual stays running from the top rear mount to the axle.

I'll extend the pennant pole upward from the sissy bar top, pushing total bike height to around 1.9-2.0, giving it a flashy, tall flair accent.

For the seat, I'm lofting the frame through several z-stations to shape a thick, quilted solo-seat pan, widest around the middle and tapering toward the front and back. I'm also adding a couple of small coil springs tucked under the front of the seat for that classic chopper look.

Now I'm shifting to the fenders, working out the sweep path for the rear fender so it arcs over the wheel at a consistent radius above the tire surface.

Working out the paint logic for fender trim...

Now I'm working out the fender geometry: a low-poly ellipse with 12 sides for the rear, and for the front fender I'm figuring the angular coverage around the wheel arc and width to clear the fork legs, attaching it to the steering bone separately from the spinning wheel bone.

For the headlight, I'm sketching a lathe profile around the axis — a rounded bucket shape with a rim, dome, and back tip — to form the housing geometry.

I want a chrome bucket with an orange accent ring, a glowing lens disc facing forward, and a small arched "eyebrow" visor swept above it for that angular, Overwatch-style angry look.

Still shaping the brow plate outline... Then I'll add bar-end mirrors as round dishes on short stems, plus a gauge housing cylinder mounted on the handlebar riser.

Also placing a speedo gauge facing the rider behind the fork top, a small hex taillight housing with red glow on the rear fender, and a textured license plate plane facing backward, mounted hanging under the tail.

Working out plate position using trig at angle -75° around the rear fender, landing near v(0, 0.52, -1.33) vertical, modeled as a thin box with a texture plane in front. I'm skipping the chain guard and now placing foot pegs, considering forward-control style placement near the front fork for a chopper look.

Still refining peg geometry...

I'll skip the shifter for now and focus on fine details: adding a hinged fuel cap on the tank, plus mount hooks. I'm placing the flame decals on both tank sides with a hex emblem inside them, and positioning a gas cap near the front-top, using a surface ray cast to find the exact mounting point.

Now I'm adding underglow lighting—thin glowing cyan capsule tubes mounted under the engine cradle via small brackets—then working on the platform shape, which needs extrusion along a different axis since the default extrude direction won't produce a flat horizontal plate.

Shaping an elongated hexagon outline for the plate, then layering a thin inset tile texture on top with a slight bevel for a hex-motif plaque look.

Sizing the rectangle to 1.3×2.5 fits within the hex boundary with margin to spare. For the texture, I'll generate the hex grid pattern procedurally as an SVG path rather than relying on a raster image, since browsers can decode SVG patterns directly and this keeps things lightweight.

I want a dark navy base with lighter hex outlines and scattered orange accent cells, plus a glowing cyan or orange strip inset along the base edge for visual polish. For scrap props, I'll add a few small details near the rear-left—maybe a fuel canister with an embossed X, built from a box and cylinder cap with a handle, to give the scene some grounded character without cluttering it.

Now I'm placing the extra props: a hazard-striped barrel front-right and a toolbox, checking their positions fit within the hex platform bounds given the bike wheel and pipe widths. I'm working out exact coordinates for the barrel and jerrycan so they sit naturally on the tile without overhanging awkwardly, and considering adding a small glowing hex-topped light pylon at a front corner for an Overwatch-style spawn point accent.

I'm now reviewing the API signatures I'll need for building geometry -- parts attached to the frame bone, rods between points, sweeps along paths, lofts with stations, and lathe outlines using 2D point arrays -- making sure I understand the expected argument shapes before writing the full part-by-part construction code.

Defining color palette constants...

Defining more color constants...

For the seat texture, I'm working out a quilted diamond stitching pattern using diagonal coordinate transforms, drawing stitch lines where the fractional part crosses a threshold and filling the diamonds with alternating leather tones.

Now I'm figuring out the hazard-stripe pattern, alternating orange and black bands based on floored position, and working through the sign issue with negative modulo so stripes alternate correctly regardless of coordinate sign.

Then I'm shaping the barrel geometry as a ribbed cylinder, painting it orange with a hazard band along a y-range, before moving on to writing the flame texture as an SVG shape for the vehicle's flank design.

Writing SVG code...

I want the flame decal to pop against the orange tank, so I'm considering a cream outline with a cyan inner flame for contrast rather than the usual warm palette.

Still writing flame paths...

Now completing the hexagon emblem with navy fill and orange bolt accent, then moving to the headlight lens design with radial gradients and ray details, plus sketching out the engine core and fan face concepts with chrome and blade elements.

I'm designing the license plate with a bold "ROAD RAGE" text and star accents, a glowing red hexagon tail light pattern, and planning the base tile generation before moving on to the gauge design.

Now I'm working out texture sizing for each element and thinking through the orientation parameters for the face disc helper—specifically how the "up" direction interacts with vertical versus horizontal placements when rolling the geometry.

Writing wheel function...

I realize I should rename the root joint to "chassis" to avoid shadowing the "frame" import, and define the wheel helper using the builder's joint type for the parent parameter. Now I'm working out the tire cross-section geometry with coordinate pairs for the rim and tread profile.

I'm figuring out how the lathe operation rotates this profile around the x-axis to form the tire, with the tread paint logic using the radial distance from the wheel center to color the surface correctly regardless of how the wheel spins.

Now I'm working out the lug pattern on the crown using an angular modulo function for 28 evenly spaced lugs, plus a sidewall stripe band positioned by radial distance, before moving on to lathe the rim barrel shape.

For the rim design, I'm deciding to make the rim chrome-colored and swap plain spokes for chunky orange bars, considering using box-shaped rods or a frustum shape to build sturdy spoke geometry.

Still working out the spoke geometry...

Still working out the neon ring placement relative to the rim barrel and inner radius...

Now I'm adding the brake disc on the front wheel using a lathed chrome shape positioned on the mount side, sized to fit inside the rim, plus an orange caliper box positioned near the top of the disc along the fork slider.

Setting hub length to span past the tire with the disc placed at x=0.072, and fixing front wheel dimensions at W=0.13, rimW=0.09. For the rear wheel, I'm working out placement of the sprocket and disc relative to the wider tire and stays, checking that the sprocket and disc sit just outside the tire while the stays attach further out near the axle ends.

Now I'm verifying the stay doesn't collide with the rear sprocket disc by tracing its path from the frame down to the axle and checking clearance at the crossing point — it clears with margin. Then I move to sizing the front (engine) and rear sprockets using module and tooth count to get pitch diameters, setting their positions relative to the crankcase and rear axle, and starting the chain length calculation based on center distance.

I'm now checking the gear geometry generator's rim and spoke sizing rules against the rear sprocket's dimensions to confirm the spokes will render properly, computing rim thickness and hub clearance, then positioning the sprocket at the rear wheel joint with the correct orientation and metal coloring.

Next I'm working out the cylinder head and exhaust port positions using vectors from the crank center along the front and rear cylinder directions.

Checking the gap between cylinders at that height, the air cleaner at radius .11 won't actually fit between them, so I'll shift it off to the side instead, placing its mount around x -0.17, y 0.66.

Now I'm working out the exhaust pipe start points -- figuring out where the ports sit on the front of each cylinder head, calculating position offsets based on cylinder radius and direction vectors, and considering whether both cylinders need pipes on both sides.

Mapping out the exhaust pipe routing coordinates...

Thinking through the heat shield as a slightly larger sweep over part of the pipe path, maybe with paint stripe styling, and adjusting the radius arrays so the shield radius stays sensible relative to the main pipe's tapered radius near the end.

I'm leaning toward splitting the construction into two separate sweeps -- one for the pipe body and one for the tip -- and adding a glowing cyan disc inside the megaphone opening, with the sweep caps set to leave that end open rather than closed.

Now I'm checking placement details: the pipe end sits near the rear fender and license plate without colliding, and the tips flare outward symmetrically. Next I need to plan handlebar geometry and grips, using a curved bar path with chrome shading and a grip rod attached at the bar's end.

Adding small lever rods and mirror stem geometry...

Now I'm working out the mirror shape as a flattened cylinder facing backward, and the riser positioning near the tree with the handlebar path starting slightly offset from center.

For the triple tree top, I'm adding a box aligned with the fork axis, oriented along the direction from the fork top to its lower point, placed partway down that line.

Still positioning more parts...

For the flames, I'm finding the tank's surface hit point using an around/center approach, placing one flame at azimuth 90 (right side, +X) and mirroring for the left side at azimuth -90, then applying the decal with appropriate size and orientation based on the hit normal.

Now I'm considering fender decals -- thinking about adding hex emblems to the rear fender sides, but the fender's thin edge geometry makes placement tricky there, so I'm deciding to skip that and instead look at putting emblems on the sissy bar area.

Then I'm weighing other emblem placements: the pennant flag, the headlight bucket, or the tank top and engine's primary cover, settling on the primary cover and pad as better options since those are flatter surfaces. I'm also planning the pennant flag shape as an extruded swallowtail outline on a pole.

Now I'm adding the pole rising from the sissy bar to a glowing finial sphere, then shaping the sissy bar itself as a swept curve starting near the rear seat stays.

Still calculating strut geometry...

Still defining fork geometry...

Now I'm working through the kickstand joint placement, anchoring it to the chassis and aiming it toward a target point to set its orientation.

For lighting, I'm adding small glowing amber spheres for turn signals, positioning them on rods extending from the headlight bracket sides so they read as mounted lenses rather than floating pieces, then starting on the rear turn signal setup.

For the taillight, I'm placing a hexagonal glowing red cylinder at the end of the fender sweep, working out the trigonometry so it sits just above where the fender curves end, and positioning a license plate hanging slightly below the tail assembly.

Then I'm checking that the plate clears the rear tire by about six centimeters, attaching it with small bracket rods to the fender end, and considering whether to add an oil tank cylinder tucked under the seat area, deciding that's probably enough detail for the frame accessories like engine mount bolts.

Thinking about stylized extras now—maybe skip the skull ornament and boar tusks, but could add a hex-vent orange detail on the tank for flair. I'm adding teal underglow capsule rods beneath the cradle with bracket rods connecting up to the rails, double-checking the tires still sit at the lowest ground point, and starting a rough part count across wheels, fork, bars, engine, and exhaust.

I'm tallying the remaining parts—frame, tank, seat, fenders, lights, platform, props—landing around 270 total, then working out a glow ring at the base using a scaled hexagon outline as a closed polyline, accepting that the seam at a vertex will produce overlapping rounded caps there.

For the base extrusion, I'm checking that the thickness direction computed from the plane vectors centers correctly on the origin point, and confirming the bevel size stays within half the thickness so it doesn't clip. I'm also considering adding a second, slightly larger base layer as a chamfered skirt beneath the first for more visual depth.

I'm settling on a two-layer base: a black hex layer from 0 to .026 at full scale, and a thinner navy layer above it at .95 scale from .026 to .04, with a glow ring at .9 scale on top and the tile plane sitting just below that. I'm defining the hexagon outline as six points forming a sharp-cornered hex shape, then checking the front wheel's forward extent based on its radius and position.

I'm verifying that the hex half-width stays wide enough at the front and rear extremes to clear the wheel and license plate, then checking that prop placements (barrel, jerry can, pylon) stay within the hex boundary at their respective z-positions without overlapping the glow ring, nudging the barrel's x-position slightly inward to avoid a collision.

I'm deciding to keep prop detailing simple, skipping extra crates or a banner board, and considering a small emblem decal on the jerry can or barrel before moving into writing the actual Three.js code.

Setting up imports and builder helpers...

Still defining helper math utilities and vector types for interpolation and lerping, plus sketching out the module-level texture generation functions...

Now I'm starting the main build function, setting up the chassis joint and fork geometry for the chopper's steering, debating which joints should carry hinge roles versus which to leave unassigned.

Writing tire paint function...

Now setting rim colors to chrome with orange spokes and neon accents, then starting a fender path function.

Writing the fender sweep curve...

Writing fender paint logic...

I'll make the tank orange on top with a navy underside using a countershade effect blending the two colors based on surface normal, giving a two-tone paint job.

For the engine, I'm planning cel-shaded aluminum fins, navy cylinder heads, and orange rocker covers, plus a lofted seat shape. Now I'm starting the final code, setting up imports for the builder, paint, toon shading, glow effects, and gauge/gear geometry helpers.

Writing hex and flame SVG paths...

Still tweaking flame path coordinates...

Still writing SVG code...

Now I'm designing a hex-core texture for the engine, using a glowing hexagon background with inner cell lines and a bright center for that energy-core look.

Still designing textures... now working out the fan blade shapes, lens gradients, tail hex pattern, and plate details for the final SVG composition.

Setting up the chassis builder with named joints for steering and rear swingarm, then writing a generic wheel-building function that handles radius, width, height and rim parameters for both front and rear wheels.

Writing the tire and rim lathe profiles...

Checking rim widths work out for both front and rear wheels against the tire half-height so the flange stays visible. The lathe outline closes the loop properly between inner edge points, and now I'm moving on to the fork geometry, building the two symmetric strut positions from the fork top point.

Still writing fork rods...

Still placing bars and gauge, now checking whether the gauge cylinder at that height might overlap with the headlight.

Shaping the headlight housing with a lathe profile running out from the axis and back, then adding a lens circle in front of it.

Building the orange rim ring as a swept torus shape, then starting the brow outline as a concave extruded polygon above the lens.

Now I'm defining the engine as a frustum box between two points, working out the orientation so width runs along local X and height along the bone's forward-up axis.

Adding cylinder fins and engine details...

Checking the air cleaner against the rocker covers, cylinder heads, and fuel tank bottom for clearance, everything seems to fit without overlap given the current coordinates.

Now I'm setting up the air cleaner shape itself—a lathe-generated body with a chrome finish, a face disc textured as a fan, then shifting over to the hex-core bracket on the right side using a six-sided cylinder prism.

For the glowing hex core face, I realize CircleGeometry with 6 segments naturally forms a hexagon, so I can use that shape with a teal glow and the HEXCORE texture mapped onto it instead of building a separate hex mesh.

Then I'm positioning the primary cover as an orange cylinder on the right side with an emblem disc, checking it doesn't overlap the air cleaner, and verifying clearance against the sprocket's radius and z-position near the cover's edge.

I'm skipping the oil pan for now and building the frame tubes using curved sweeps along Catmull-Rom splines for the rounded sections and straight rods for the direct runs, defining the top tube's path to tuck in behind the tank where it's still partially visible.

Now I'm adding the rear axle hardware -- cylinder geometries for the axle plates and the main axle rod running through the wheel hub, all chrome and attached to the wheelR bone so they spin correctly, plus the license plate and sissy bar details before moving on to heat clamps placed along the pipe sweep.

For the clamps, I'm using the path's point and tangent at each parameter t to orient torus-like cylinder rings around the pipe, with the clamp radius interpolated from a lookup array matching the pipe's tapering profile. Now I'm figuring out the heat shield geometry next.

Checking the tank's rear position against the seat front to make sure they align vertically. For the seat spring, I'm sketching a small coil beneath the seat nose, positioning its endpoints relative to the top tube height.

Realizing the top tube actually passes too high and would clip through the seat, so I need to route it lower for a hardtail-style chopper frame -- dropping the tube path under the tank and seat while checking clearances at each z-station to confirm it stays clear of both components.

That's close enough to pass as mounted overlap. I'll skip adding springs to avoid extra collision risk, and leave the coil geometry out entirely to keep things simple.

Defining the rear stays with a curved sweep from the spine down to the swingarm area, then thinking about whether to add a small battery box under the seat — probably skip it for now too.

I'm skipping the battery box and instead adding the drive chain as top and bottom rods connecting a front sprocket near the chassis to a rear sprocket at the rear wheel, both thin black cylinders positioned at calculated offsets.

Now I'm positioning the rear wheel and disc, placing the rear disc on the lathe geometry aligned with the wheel center, then adding a fixed caliper box in orange near the bottom-front of the disc, plus checking exhaust pipe clearance against the rear wheel and disc radius before moving on to the foot pegs.

Shift lever and pylon/props are being skipped for now. I'm adding a hexagonal taillight cylinder glowing red at the rear, then working out the fender's trailing curve point to make sure it clears the tire radius with a small margin before extending the tail section further back.

I'm placing the taillight just below the fender's end, adding a license plate beneath it with its own bottom clearance above the floor, and now working out mounting rods to bracket the plate in place.

Still writing plate geometry...

Now I'm adding platform hazard props: a barrel with ribbed rings and a lid using cylinder primitives, plus plans for a jerrycan and pylon.

Now I'm sketching a pylon with a navy pole, a hexagonal glowing teal head, and a wider base cylinder. I'm double-checking the color palette count stays reasonable, confirming the gauge texture size default works, and verifying that decal targets can accept surfaces built from lofted/swept geometry like the tank.
